item.title: Bill for Birmingham's Oracle debacle reaches £128M
item.description: Birmingham City Council faces a £128.1 million bill for its disastrous transition from SAP to Oracle – more than six times the original estimate for a project that contributed to its financial collapse. Papers presented to its Audit Committee this week put the combined cost of the original implementation, which went live in 2022, and this year's reimplementation at £128.1 million, against £19.96 million forecast in the 2019 business case [PDF]. The report , from program director Philip Macpherson, said the project's funding allocation had previously reached £157 million. The report said the new Oracle Fusion system went live in August without any priority-one or "showstopper" issues. "The program has now moved into the Post Go Live Support phase where [it] continues to provide extra support but slowly transitions towards 'Business As Usual' operating procedures," the report said. It is an understatement to say the same was not true of the first attempt to move the council's finance, HR, and payroll systems off its legacy R/3 SAP system to more modern software. The first project started in 2019 and was supposed to go live in April 2021, but was delayed by a year. After the council started to use the system in April 2022, it soon became beset by a series of serious problems. Although the council had planned to implement Oracle "out-of-the-box," it created several customizations, including a bank reconciliation system that failed to function properly. The council struggled to understand its cash position and was unable to produce auditable accounts . It has spent more than £5 million on manual workaround labor . The system move also contributed to it becoming effectively bankrupt , an event it failed to foresee due to the malfunctioning finance system. It later emerged that officials ignored a "red" warning prior to the go-live date. They were explicitly told the system could cause late payments, a failure to collect debt, and incorrect accounting if it went live. Officials gave the go-ahead regardless. The council decided to reimplement Oracle from scratch, while running the current system as best it could and implementing off-the-shelf software CivicaPay , now rebranded as Civica Income Management. Despite the apparently trouble-free relaunch, the true cost to the council is likely higher than the projected £128.1 million implementation bill. For a start, the original £19 million budget was supposed to support the software implementation for schools , but that was excluded from the reimplementation. Secondly, the council expected significant savings from moving to Oracle in 2022 through greater efficiency. The 2019 business case booked £27 million in savings from 2019 to 2031, for example. A 2024 analysis by Audit Reform Lab, based at the University of Sheffield, estimated that the disaster's direct and indirect financial impact, including lost savings and deteriorating tax collection, would reach £216.5 million by April 2026. item.description: By Adegboyega Adeleye African Democratic Congress (ADC) deputy governorship candidate Babatunde Olalere Gbadamosi has projected that the party’s waste management plan would create at least 21,000 jobs in Lagos, including 20,000 for waste collection crews. Gbadamosi, who is running with ADC governorship candidate Gbadebo Rhodes-Vivour, spoke at the Road to Election 2027 Lagos Deputy Governorship Debate on Nigeria Info FM on Friday, where he outlined proposals on employment, waste collection, housing and transportation. Addressing unemployment, Gbadamosi said he did not know the state’s unemployment rate and disputed figures published by the Lagos government. He proposed a review of public sector salaries and said his plans for waste management, housing, transportation and education would create jobs for Lagosians. “First of all, the truth is, I suppose the truth is, I really don’t know what the unemployment rate is. Whatever figures that are put out by the APC government of Lagos State are usually just false. They just manufacture figures, yank them out of their a**,” he said. He said he and Rhodes-Vivour had agreed to “undertake a review, a wholesale review of public sector salaries, in order to bring them in line with our current economic realities.” He also cited plans for 20,000 jobs in waste-to-energy, 100,000 affordable housing units and 16,000 electric buses. “We plan to bring 16,000 electric buses into Lagos State because we simply don’t have enough capacity to carry the 24 million people of Lagos State on the current transportation system,” he said, adding that the housing and transport plans would also provide work for young people. On waste collection, Gbadamosi proposed providing each local government with at least 200 dumpsters. He estimated that 4,000 trucks, each with a five-person crew, would create 20,000 jobs. “All right, we have 20 local governments. So 200 times 20, that’s 4000 trucks. 4000 trucks times five crew members, each. That’s already 20,000 jobs,” he said. He estimated that recycling centres would create at least another 1,000 jobs, based on a minimum of 50 workers at each of 20 local government centres. “That’s 50 jobs times 20 local governments. That’s already what 1000 extra jobs minimum,” he said, adding that the programme would be funded with “25% of Lagos State revenue that is being paid to Alpha Beta at the moment.” Other major contenders at the debate included Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) deputy governorship candidate Moriam Tolani Animashaun and Social Democratic Party (SDP) deputy candidate Kayode Evelyn Aderiyike. The debate was hosted by Kofi Bartels and Ireti Bakare-Yusuf. The post ADC waste plan will create 21,000 jobs in Lagos – Gbadamosi appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: PANDEF rejects 20% NCDMB fund deduction for research council
item.description: …Warns against diversion of local content funds, urges NASS to review proposed legislation By Henry Umoru ABUJA – The Pan Niger Delta Forum (PANDEF), the apex socio-political body of the South-South geopolitical zone, has rejected the proposed 20 per cent deduction from the Nigerian Content Development Fund to finance the proposed National Council on Research, Science, Technology and Innovation. The forum warned that the move could undermine years of investment in indigenous industrial capacity and weaken the Nigerian Content Development and Monitoring Board (NCDMB), which has been instrumental in promoting local expertise, skills acquisition, enterprise development and industrialisation. PANDEF urged the National Assembly to review Section 19 of the proposed legislation establishing the council and reject the provision earmarking 20 per cent of the Nigerian Content Development Fund for its financing. Addressing journalists in Abuja on Friday, PANDEF National Chairman, Ambassador Godknows Igali, acknowledged the Federal Government’s efforts to strengthen the country’s research, science, technology and innovation capacity but expressed concern over Part IV, Section 19(a) of the proposed Bill. He described the proposed funding arrangement as inappropriate, counterproductive and fundamentally flawed, arguing that a new national institution should not be financed by weakening an existing statutory agency with clearly defined responsibilities and ongoing development commitments. Igali said the NCDMB, which commenced operations in 2010, had a statutory mandate to promote the development, acquisition and application of indigenous capacity in Nigeria’s oil and gas industry. He noted that the Nigerian Content Development Fund was already supporting strategic investments in the oil and gas sector and related areas, including agriculture, manufacturing and transportation. According to him, diverting 20 per cent of the fund could disrupt existing commitments, constrain ongoing investments and slow the progress recorded in local content development. “The Nigerian Content Development Fund is not an idle pool of resources awaiting allocation. It is an active development instrument that is already financing and supporting several strategic investments in the oil and gas industry and related sectors of the Nigerian economy,” he said. Igali also warned that the proposed funding mechanism could establish a dangerous precedent in public finance, whereby newly established government institutions would depend on deductions from funds already allocated to existing statutory agencies. He said such an arrangement was inconsistent with sound corporate governance and fiscal policy, stressing that new institutions should have independent, predictable and sustainable funding structures. “The principle of sound public finance requires that the establishment of new institutions should be accompanied by deliberate, independent and sustainable funding arrangements. “It is inappr

item.title: Bitcoin Price Trades Near $61,300 as Tech Stock Futures Rally
item.description: Bitcoin Magazine Bitcoin Price Trades Near $61,300 as Tech Stock Futures Rally The bitcoin price traded near $61,300 on Friday morning, as tech stock futures jumped ahead of a holiday-shortened session on Wall Street. Bitcoin price is on track for its first weekly gain after seven straight weekly losses, though it is still down about 20% in November. The bitcoin price was up about 1.7% early Friday and set to add 4.8% for the week, Investing.com reported , extending a recovery from a two-year low of $57,325.70 hit earlier in the week. Bitcoin slumped below $57,500 on Wednesday as the Nasdaq sank at the open, before a late rebound in tech shares lifted risk assets. Short sellers helped fuel the bounce. Shorts made up 77% of $84.7 million in bitcoin liquidations over the past day, while futures open interest was little changed. That suggests forced short covering, rather than fresh leverage, supplied much of the lift. Tech futures lead the risk rebound Nasdaq 100 futures rose 2.2% by 6:42 a.m. ET, Reuters reported, as investors returned from Thanksgiving and piled back into battered AI-linked shares. Nvidia gained 3.6% in premarket trading, while AMD climbed 4.4% and Broadcom added 3.4%. S&P 500 futures rose 1.6%, and Dow futures gained 1.3%. “There have been some signs that the tech selloff has stabilised for now, and that risk appetite is returning to markets,” Deutsche Bank analysts said in a note cited by Reuters. The S&P 500 is headed for its best week since April, though it remains on course for its worst November since 2008. Bitcoin price has followed that rebound but lagged it. The major U.S. stock indexes are each up around 4% on the week, and silver jumped about 7% to above $44 an ounce on Friday while gold added 2.5% to above $3,670. Stocks close early at 1 p.m. ET, and the bond market shuts at 2 p.m. Rate hike bets and ETF outflows linger The macro backdrop still weighs on the bitcoin price. Traders are almost fully pricing in a Federal Reserve rate hike in December after data this week showed the economy grew faster than first estimated in the third quarter and inflation accelerated in October, Reuters reported. Third-quarter GDP growth was revised up to 4.3%, and the 10-year Treasury yield slipped to 4.84%. Spot bitcoin ETFs are also still losing cash. The U.S. funds lost $453 million on Wednesday, their seventh straight day of outflows, with BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust accounting for $329.7 million. That pushed November outflows to about $5.39 billion, extending what was already a record month for the funds. Crypto stocks and miners in focus Crypto stocks face their own test in Friday’s short session. Strategy shares rose 3.1% to $79.96 on Wednesday, while Coinbase gained 1.3% to $103.72. Bitcoin miners that have moved into AI hosting tracked the tech rally, with IREN and Cipher Digital each gaining 8% in premarket trading. Mining economics remain tight with the bitcoin price this low. CleanSpark has weighed selling more bitcoi

item.title: Galaxy Withdraws Call That Bitcoin’s Bear Market Ended in June
item.description: Bitcoin Magazine Galaxy Withdraws Call That Bitcoin’s Bear Market Ended in June Galaxy has withdrawn its October call that bitcoin’s bear market ended in June, saying the technical signal behind it failed after seven straight weeks of losses and that the bear market is “very likely not over.” Alex Thorn, Galaxy’s head of firmwide research, laid out the reversal in a report published Wednesday and sent to clients a day earlier. “We withdraw our call that the bear market ended in June,” the report said. “The signal it rested on has failed.” The firm’s Oct. 26 note had argued that bitcoin had entered an accumulation phase. Galaxy said at the time that a weekly close back below the 50-week moving average that was not regained within a month would invalidate its technical case. That is what happened. Bitcoin closed the week ended Nov. 8 at $74,968, 0.7% below the 50-week average, after seven weekly closes above it. It then closed the week ended Nov. 15 below the 200-week average, which Galaxy has described as the floor of past bear markets. Galaxy points to $58,525 The week ended Nov. 22 closed at $61,104, 17.9% below the 50-week average and 10.4% below the 200-week average of $68,159. Bitcoin traded below its July 1 intraday low on Nov. 20 and reached $55,100 on Nov. 21, but the June 30 closing low of $58,525 held on a daily basis through Nov. 22. Galaxy now treats that level as the line to watch. A daily close below $58,525 would be “the start of a move to a materially lower low,” the report said, and the firm would not treat such a close as a buying signal by itself. History is not kind to breaks like that. In the seven prior bear market cases where bitcoin closed below a low that had stood for at least 60 days, the eventual low was at least 17% lower, with a median of 52%. Applied to the June low, that works out to about $48,500 and $28,200. Bitcoin briefly slumped below $57,500 on Wednesday morning as the Nasdaq sank, but it ended the day back above $60,000 and has not posted a daily close below $58,525. It traded near $60,800 on Thursday morning. Late by the clock, early by the depth Galaxy said two readings of the market disagree. By the calendar, this bear is old: Nov. 22 was day 412 since the Oct. 6, 2025, record, longer than the 163 to 406 days from high to low in the four prior bear markets. By depth, it looks unfinished. Bitcoin’s 53% decline compares with drops of 77% to 93% in earlier bears. It also has not closed a day below its realized price of $53,205, something every prior bear did for at least 140 days, and only two of the 13 bottom signals Galaxy tracks have been met. “The clock says this bear is overdue to end, the depth says it has further to fall, and we do not believe the price record alone can settle which,” the report said. Flows have not helped. Galaxy estimates U.S. spot bitcoin ETPs hold about 1.24 million BTC, 9.7% below their October 2025 peak, after shedding 71,339 BTC, or $4.95 billion, since Oct. 4. November is shapi

item.title: The Oura Ring 5 just got its biggest discount ever for Black Friday
item.description: The Oura Ring 5 is smaller and more comfortable to wear than the Ring 4 (surprise, surprise). | Photo: Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge If you’ve been curious about smart rings but have been put off by their high price tags, Black Friday is a good time to consider giving one a try. That’s because the Oura Ring 5 , which we consider the best smart ring you can buy, has dropped to an all-time low of $299 ($100 off) at Amazon , Best Buy , Walmart , and Oura’s online storefront for Black Friday. Oura Ring 5 Where to Buy: $399 $299 at Amazon $399 $299 at Walmart $399 $299 at Best Buy Compared to the Ring 4 , the Oura Ring 5 offers a thinner, lighter, and more durable design that’s more comfortable to wear throughout the day and while sleeping. Like its predecessor, it can track your sleep, activity, heart rate, and other health metrics, giving you insights into your overall well-being without requiring you to constantly check a screen. It also offers roughly the same battery life and sensors as the prior model, though its new charging case supports wireless charging. (Unfortunately, the case is currently sold separately for $99 .) Oura has also introduced several new software features, including Health Radar, which looks for potentially significant changes in your health. You can also import medical lab results, track GLP-1 medications, and access AI-assisted medical guidance through Oura’s partnership with Counsel Health. My colleague Victoria Song appreciated how the latter makes it easier to connect with an actual doctor, though she found it better suited for quick medical questions than more serious health concerns. However, none of these software features are exclusive to the Ring 5, and you’ll still need a $5.99 monthly Oura membership to access most of its health insights. Given how similar the two generations are, we wouldn’t recommend upgrading if you already own a Ring 4. But if you’re new to smart rings, the current discount makes Oura’s latest model much more attractive, especially since it’s only $50 more than the Ring 4’s starting price. Read our full Oura Ring 5 review .

Governor Adeleke spoke while addressing hundreds of dignitaries and residents who thronged the Osogbo township stadium to be part of his inauguration. item.title: UK government rejects national consultation on AI datacenters
item.description: The UK government has rejected calls for a UK-wide public consultation on the environmental impacts of AI datacenters, despite a petition attracting more than 39,000 signatures. Campaign group Protect the Wild launched the petition last month, calling for a national consultation that would consider whether further expansion should be restricted, paused, or halted until those impacts are properly understood and addressed. The nonprofit says the petition smashed the 10,000 signature threshold above which a government response is required in just three days, and the total stood at over 39,000 as this article was being prepared. In its response, published on November 23, the government ruled out the requested UK-wide environmental consultation, saying individual projects' impacts should be addressed through the planning process. It pointed instead to a separate consultation on its draft datacenter planning policy, open until January 8, 2027. "Datacenters are vital to the UK's digital economy. They underpin the digital services that people rely on every day, including public services, healthcare and the way people work. They also provide the infrastructure needed to develop and use AI," the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (BIST) says. "Building more capacity in the UK will support economic growth and innovation, while strengthening national resilience and ensuring the UK is well placed to realize the opportunities presented by AI." But it adds that the government recognizes the environmental impacts of bit barns are real and must be understood and mitigated, and this is one of the reasons why it established the Data Centre Covenant tests. This Covenant, published last month, sets out tests all compute sheds "are encouraged to meet," while "strategic datacenters" are required to meet them to qualify for additional government assistance. The government has yet to define which datacenters qualify as "strategic," saying it will publish further details and eligibility criteria in due course. Qualifying projects could receive help securing power and accelerating planning. Briefly, the Covenant tests are that operators cover any energy costs they create, so that communities do not have to pick up the bill; that they invest in local communities; adhere to the highest environmental standards; create jobs and drive reindustrialization; and provide secure and reliable access to their compute resources. If this has a ring of familiarity, it is because President Trump earlier this year introduced a Ratepayer Protection Pledge , under which hyperscalers and AI companies agreed to protect US consumers from any bill shocks due to the energy and infrastructure requirements of their datacenter projects. It seems that where the US leads, the UK still often follows. The Covenant sets out efficiency targets and reporting expectations, but does not explain how compliance will be enforced or specify penalties for failing to meet its tests. Protect the

item.title: [PHOTOS] Adeleke Sworn In For Second Term As Osun Governor
item.description: Osun State Governor, Ademola Adeleke, has been sworn in for a second term, beginning another four-year tenure that will run until 2030. Adeleke took the oath of office on Friday, November 27, 2026, at an inauguration ceremony held at the Osogbo Township Stadium. The state Chief Judge administered the oath of office to Deputy Governor Kola Adewusi before swearing in Adeleke. The ceremony was attended by Vice President Kashim Shettima, who led several dignitaries, including former Osun State Governor Bisi Akande, Ondo State Governor Lucky Aiyedatiwa, and former Senate President Bukola Saraki. The entertainment industry was also represented, with Afrobeats singer Davido, alongside B-Red and Shina Rambo, attending the ceremony to celebrate the governor. Adeleke secured re-election in the August 15, 2026 governorship election on the platform of the Accord Party after defecting from the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP). item.title: Full list: African countries where travelers can access without visa
item.description: Travelling across Africa is becoming easier as more countries adopt visa-free entry policies aimed at promoting tourism, strengthening regional integration and encouraging trade among African nations. Several African countries have introduced policies allowing citizens of other African countries to visit without obtaining a visa before travelling, reducing the cost and administrative hurdles associated with cross-border movement. Among the countries offering such access are Benin, The Gambia, Rwanda, Seychelles, Ghana and Togo. The policies form part of wider efforts to improve freedom of movement across the continent and advance the African Union’s goal of greater economic integration. The six countries are highlighted below, although their entry arrangements are not identical. 1. Benin Benin is one of Africa’s leading supporters of visa-free movement. It allows citizens of other African countries to enter without obtaining a visa before travelling. The country has promoted easier cross-border movement to encourage tourism, business and regional cooperation. 2. The Gambia The Gambia offers visa-free entry to citizens of other African countries. It is one of the continent’s more open destinations, making it attractive to visitors interested in tourism, business and cultural exchanges. 3. Rwanda Rwanda allows citizens of African Union member states to enter without a visa. The policy supports the country’s efforts to attract African visitors, investors and business travellers. 4. Seychelles Seychelles operates a visa-free entry policy for visitors of all nationalities, including African travellers. However, visitors must obtain the required travel authorisation before departure and meet the country’s entry conditions. 5. Ghana Ghana introduced a free visa policy for African nationals in May 2026. Under the arrangement, African travellers can apply for electronic visas without paying visa fees. However, an application and approval are still required, meaning the policy is not strictly visa-free entry. 6. Togo Togo has introduced visa-free entry for African passport holders, subject to pre-arrival requirements. The policy is part of efforts to facilitate movement across the continent and strengthen regional integration. item.title: Kano govt to Kwankwaso: Stop dragging Yusuf into EFCC troubles
item.description: By Hadiza Yusuf The Kano State Government has asked former Governor Rabiu Musa Kwankwaso to stop linking Governor Abba Kabir Yusuf to his alleged dealings with the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC). The government said Yusuf had no involvement in Kwankwaso’s issues with the anti-graft agency, which it claimed predated the current administration. The Commissioner for Information and Internal Affairs, Sunusi Bature Dawakin Tofa, stated this in a statement issued on Friday. He described Kwankwaso’s allegations against the governor as misleading and politically motivated. According to the government, it was wrong for the former governor to accuse Yusuf of influencing the EFCC investigation when the matter began before his administration. “The crisis and court cases involving the NDC are internal party matters arising from disagreements among its members, and the Kano State Government has no involvement in them,” the statement said. The government accused Kwankwaso of using the governor as a target to gain public sympathy and remain politically relevant ahead of the 2027 general elections. “Rather than constantly blaming the Kano State Government for his political difficulties, Kwankwaso should concentrate on resolving the internal challenges confronting his political camp,” the statement said. It maintained that Yusuf was elected to govern Kano State and deliver development, not to engage in political arguments or take responsibility for the problems of other political parties. The government urged Kwankwaso to allow the administration to focus on fulfilling its promises to the people, warning that attempts to gain public sympathy through political blackmail would not succeed. “You cannot win public sympathy through blackmail and unfounded allegations,” it said. The statement added that the people of Kano State would have the opportunity to judge political leaders through their votes in 2027. It further reaffirmed that Yusuf remained committed to governance, development and the welfare of residents. Recall that Kwankwaso had accused Governor Yusuf of using the EFCC and other government institutions to target him and members of his family for political reasons ahead of the 2027 elections. He also alleged that the governor attempted to pressure the EFCC through protests at its office and interfere in a case involving the NDC governorship candidate. The post Kano govt to Kwankwaso: Stop dragging Yusuf into EFCC troubles appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: Obasanjo unhappy Tinubu is delivering on promises — FHA director
item.description: B y Dapo Akinrefon An Executive Director (Projects Implementation) of the Federal Housing Authority (FHA), Oluremi Omowaiye, has criticised former President Olusegun Obasanjo over his remarks on President Bola Tinubu’s economic reforms, alleging that the former president was uncomfortable with the achievements of the current administration. Omowaiye, who defended Tinubu’s economic policies, said Obasanjo was unhappy because the President had achieved what he failed to accomplish during his eight years in office. Obasanjo had criticised the Tinubu administration’s economic reforms, arguing that they had pushed many Nigerians deeper into poverty. However, reacting to the former president’s position in a statement on Friday, Omowaiye, a chieftain of the All Progressives Congress (APC), said Obasanjo should be ashamed of his comments, insisting that Tinubu had surpassed his achievements. “Obasanjo should cover his face in shame. He is unhappy because we have Yoruba man who has done what he failed to do as president. He is uncomfortable because President Tinubu has surpassed his achievements,” he said. The FHA director further alleged that Obasanjo was uncomfortable with Tinubu’s performance because the President was delivering on his promises and could secure another four-year term in 2027. “Obasanjo is unhappy because President Tinubu is delivering on his promises and he knows he is going to achieve much more when he gets reelected for another four years. That is why he is doing everything to stop it but he won’t succeed. “Nigerians are happy with the President’s Renewed Hope agenda and they want him to continue,” Omowaiye said. Questioning Obasanjo’s claim that Tinubu’s reforms had made Nigerians 300 per cent poorer, Omowaiye argued that the former president’s business interests continued to operate despite the economic difficulties he had highlighted. He specifically cited Bells University and Obasanjo Farms, asking whether the former president had shut down either business because of the financial challenges facing Nigerians. “Did he close down Bells University because students are unable to pay? No. Has he closed down Obasanjo Farms because the economy is so bad?” he asked. Omowaiye also cited Next Cash and Carry supermarket, which he described as Nigeria’s biggest single supermarket, arguing that its continued operation after a fire incident demonstrated that businesses could still thrive despite economic challenges. “Peter Obi that Obasanjo is supporting has the biggest single supermarket in Nigeria. It got burnt sometimes ago. He rebuilt it and it is doing fine today. If the economy is so bad, will Next Supermarket be doing fine?” he queried. He also faulted Obasanjo over the state of infrastructure during his presidency, particularly the Lagos-Ibadan Expressway, which he described as the country’s most economically viable road. item.title: Tyson Fury’s wife withdraws claim that boxer has schizophrenia
item.description: Paris Fury, the wife of British heavyweight boxer Tyson Fury, has withdrawn her earlier claim that her husband was diagnosed with schizophrenia, clarifying that he has never been formally diagnosed with the condition. Paris made the clarification after an earlier version of an upcoming Netflix documentary about the boxer featured her describing him as having “mild schizophrenia”. In a statement, she said she had used the term while recalling a conversation about Tyson’s mental health struggles several years ago, but acknowledged that it was not an accurate description of his medical history. “I want to clarify a statement I made in the original version of the Tyson Fury documentary,” she said. “I recalled a conversation from many years ago when discussing Tyson’s condition and I used the word ‘schizophrenic’. Whilst Tyson did show some symptoms associated with schizophrenia, he doesn’t have this condition and has never received a diagnosis.” She added that mental health was complex and that finding the right words to describe someone’s experiences was not always easy. “Mental health is complex, and it isn’t always easy to find the right words, especially when you’re living it with someone you love,” she said. Paris also praised her husband for speaking openly about his struggles and thanked the public for supporting their family. Netflix confirmed that it had updated the documentary following the family’s clarification about Tyson’s official mental health diagnosis. “Following new information shared by the family relating to Tyson’s official mental health diagnosis, we have worked alongside them to update the documentary accordingly ahead of launch,” the streaming platform said. The earlier comments had attracted attention from the British Boxing Board of Control, which indicated that it was investigating the matter. The 38 year old boxer is scheduled to face Joshua in an all British heavyweight showdown in Cardiff on December 11, with the vacant WBA title expected to be at stake. Tyson has previously spoken publicly about his mental health struggles following his victory over Ukraine’s Wladimir Klitschko in 2015, when he became world heavyweight champion. After the victory, he took a break of nearly three years from boxing, during which he battled suicidal thoughts, drug and alcohol problems, and significant weight gain. Reflecting on that period in the documentary, Tyson said he experienced severe psychological distress. “Words can’t explain the darkness I was in,” he said. “I came from the living version of the pits of hellfire. And I 100 percent thought at times I’d end up in a padded room with the door locked, and that scared me so much.” He later returned to boxing and regained the world heavyweight title by defeating Deontay Wilder in February 2020. Tyson suffered the first two defeats of his professional career against Oleksandr Usyk in 2024, leaving him with 39 professional fights on his record. The post Tyson Fury’s wife withdraws claim

item.title: Lloyds and Bank of Scotland apps fall over on payday
item.description: Lloyds Bank and Bank of Scotland customers reported problems accessing online banking and transferring money on Friday morning. Reports on Downdetector began rising around 1000 UTC. Lloyds also acknowledged problems on its service status page . A reader who supplied the screenshot below noted the particularly awkward timing: the last Friday of the month is payday for many workers. One customer tweeted that she had "no food at home and cannot shop because I cannot transfer funds from my secondary Lloyds account to my main one. At this point I'm just going to withdraw every penny the moment I'm paid, so much for Internet banking. Never had this years ago." Bank of Scotland, another Lloyds Banking Group brand, reported similar problems on its service status page : " We're aware some customers are having issues with our app and online banking at the moment. We're sorry about this and are working hard to fix it." Earlier this year, a botched overnight software update at Lloyds Banking Group potentially exposed other customers' transaction information to almost 448,000 app users. In a letter to Parliament's Treasury Committee, consumer relationships CEO Jasjyot Singh blamed a defect in the API handling transaction data. The incident affected Lloyds, Halifax, and Bank of Scotland, and prompted goodwill payments to thousands of customers. Lloyds Banking Group said late last year that it had more than 21 million mobile app users and over 23 million digitally active customers. A spokesperson for Lloyds Banking Group told The Register : "We're aware some customers are having difficulty accessing the app this morning. We’re sorry for the inconvenience and are working to get things back to normal as quickly as possible." ®

item.title: Arsenic In The Water: Thailand Presses Myanmar Over Mining Pollution
item.description: As pollution mounts in its rivers, food and water, Thailand is pressing neighbouring Myanmar to tackle unregulated mining, while urging China to exert its influence in the war-ravaged nation. Tap water supplies to 14 villages in Mae Sai district near the Myanmar border were suspended earlier this month after arsenic levels were found to be nearly 30 times government limits. Bangkok this week hosted the first Thai-Myanmar working group on the issue — also attended by the Chinese ambassador — where it said tests proved rare-earth and gold mines in Myanmar were causing the pollution downstream. The two sides agreed to joint water sampling on the Kok and Sai rivers. This photo taken on June 5, 2026 shows Wan Wiriya, assistant professor from Chiang Mai University, showing the results of an arsenic level test from a water sample (C) taken from the Kok River, next to a control sample of drinking water (R) near the the northern Thai city of Chiang Rai. Photo by LILLIAN SUWANRUMPHA / AFP But there was no public agreement to Thailand’s request for a six-month suspension of operations, and how one could be implemented remains unclear, with Myanmar’s military not in full control. Bangkok is also looking to China, the main importer of rare-earth materials from Myanmar, to pressure private Chinese operators, as a months-long concern becomes increasingly urgent. Authorities warned residents this week against eating certain shellfish and other river species after tests in northern and northeastern Thailand found dangerous levels of arsenic and lead. Saengwaree Suvirakan, a farmer from Tha Ton in Chiang Mai province who joined a protest in Bangkok this week, said fish stocks were declining in any case. “Now with the mines the fish are all gone,” she said. ‘Not from nature’ This photo taken on June 4, 2026 shows fishermen and their boats near the confluence of the Kok River and Mekong River in Chiang Saen, northern Thailand’s Chiang Rai province. Photo by LILLIAN SUWANRUMPHA / AFP At the joint talks, Thai ministers said high arsenic levels in the Kok and Sai rivers could only have come from rare-earth and gold mines on the Myanmar side. “Arsenic does not come from nature, it came from mining sites. The source was from (Myanmar’s) Shan state, no-one disagrees,” Science Minister Yodchanan Wongsawat said. But how to tackle it remains an issue. Thanapon Piman, senior research fellow at the Stockholm Environment Institute (SEI), welcomed the agreement on joint sampling sites. “This is going to be a first step to agree on the evidence, otherwise you cannot move to the next step, like stopping mining activity,” he told AFP. But Myanmar intervening to stop mining would be “really difficult”, he added. Multiple ethnic armed groups have been operating there for decades, while a 2021 military coup sparked an ongoing civil war. Thai officials pinpointed two gold mines just over the border from Mae Sai as the main source of high arsenic levels in the Sai River. Different group

item.title: Full list: Italy unveils 14 African countries eligible for work visas
item.description: Italy has listed 14 African countries whose citizens are eligible to apply for work visas under its 2026–2028 immigration programme, offering employment opportunities to foreign workers across several sectors of its economy. Nigeria is among the African countries on the list, alongside Ghana, Senegal, Morocco, Egypt and 10 others. The programme forms part of Italy’s broader labour migration policy, which seeks to admit foreign workers to address labour shortages and meet the country’s employment needs. Under the programme, the Italian government has reserved 25,000 work permits annually for citizens of 38 designated countries, including the 14 African nations. The African countries named are: Algeria Ivory Coast Egypt Ethiopia The Gambia Ghana Mali Morocco Mauritius Niger Nigeria Senegal Sudan Tunisia. The employment opportunities cover sectors including agriculture, forestry, fishing, food production, manufacturing, construction, wholesale and retail trade, hospitality, tourism, transportation, logistics, healthcare and social assistance. According to the Italian Ministry of Labour and Social Policies, the immigration programme provides for a total of 497,550 foreign workers to enter Italy between 2026 and 2028. The allocation is divided into 164,850 workers for 2026, 165,850 for 2027 and 166,850 for 2028. The figures cover seasonal and non-seasonal employment as well as self-employment. However, inclusion on the list does not automatically guarantee a work visa. Applicants must secure employment from an Italian employer, who is generally required to apply for the relevant work authorisation, known as nulla osta , before the worker proceeds with the visa application. For the 2026 allocation, applications for seasonal agricultural jobs were scheduled to open on January 12, while those for seasonal tourism jobs were scheduled for February 9. Applications for non-seasonal employment under the relevant categories were scheduled for February 16 and 18, 2026. The programme is part of Italy’s efforts to address labour shortages through regulated migration while strengthening cooperation with countries of origin. item.title: UK Reform leader vows to scrap Graduate visa route used by 20,478 Nigerians
item.description: UK Reform UK leader, Nigel Farage, has vowed to scrap the United Kingdom’s Graduate visa route if his party wins power, a move that could affect thousands of Nigerians who use the scheme to remain in the country after completing their studies. Farage announced the proposal in a post on X on Thursday, arguing that the route allows foreign graduates to stay in the UK for two years after completing their degrees, competing with British workers for entry level jobs or potentially claiming asylum. Figures published by the UK Home Office on November 26 showed that 20,478 Nigerian nationals received grants under the Graduate route in the year to September 2026, making Nigerians the third largest group of beneficiaries. Indian nationals topped the list with 66,552 grants, followed by Pakistanis with 24,768. The three nationalities accounted for about 69 per cent of all grants recorded during the period. The Graduate route allows international students who have completed eligible courses at UK universities to remain in the country and work or look for employment without needing an immediate job offer or sponsorship. Reform UK’s home affairs spokesman, Zia Yusuf, has described the scheme as “a scam on the British people” and proposed replacing it with a 30 day period for graduates to secure a qualifying job that meets an economic value test. The party said about 800,000 Graduate visas, including those issued to dependants, had been granted since the route was introduced in July 2021. Yusuf also cited Home Office figures showing that 5,130 asylum claims were made by people who had previously held Graduate visas in the year to June 2026, twice the number recorded in the preceding year. The pledge comes as the Labour government is already preparing to reduce the standard duration of the Graduate visa from two years to 18 months from January 1, 2027. The change will not apply to graduates from institutions that meet certain compliance and labour market outcome standards. However, Reform UK has yet to clarify how its proposed abolition would affect people who already hold Graduate visas or international students currently studying in the country. The latest Home Office figures also showed a decline in the number of Nigerian students receiving sponsored study visas. Grants to Nigerian nationals fell by 34 per cent to 19,734 in the year to September 2026, representing about six per cent of the total. The post UK Reform leader vows to scrap Graduate visa route used by 20,478 Nigerians appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: Europe's AI sovereignty push: Lots of cloud, not much silver lining
item.description: Europe's IT spending is growing more slowly than the global average, according to Gartner, whose analysts warn that the region's push for tech sovereignty faces commercial and technological obstacles. Gartner forecasts European IT spending of $1.57 trillion in 2027, up 9.9 percent from 2026, compared with worldwide growth of 15 percent to $7.35 trillion. For 2026, it estimates spending growth of 20.7 percent in North America and 13.7 percent in China. "The world seems to be racing towards this AI goal of where the large language model provider is going to be, and the race seems to be between North American-based providers and some Asia Pacific providers," John-David Lovelock, Distinguished VP Analyst at Gartner, told The Register . He said Europe had traditionally trailed in IT uptake. "We saw that happen when global sourcing, cloud, and software as a service all came along. It's down to the pushback against the idea of creative destruction," where new technologies replace old ones. Europe's fastest growing categories are datacenter systems, forecast to grow 29.7 percent in 2027, and infrastructure as a service, at 26.7 percent. Even so, Lovelock does not expect Europe to compete with North America and China on AI investment. "For AI provision, Europe is going to be behind, and there won't be a way to catch up," he said. "The AI datacenters, the large language models, the foundational models, the tools and techniques for building out AI are all being centered outside of Europe, but enterprises don't need to do that. So the question becomes: regardless of where the source of the AI is coming from, can the enterprises actually adopt and use it? In one sense, Europe will be behind in the provision of AI, but it need not be behind in the use." The gap nonetheless complicates Europe's push to reduce its dependence on US technology suppliers. The European Union has introduced new rules to encourage tech buyers to favor sovereign tech over the dominant tech vendors, but Lovelock doubts they will move spending much. "Sovereignty is a wonderful flag that we fly on the front of a building. IT is running in the basement. CIOs are not going to buy a second-best solution that costs more simply because it's sovereign. "They are not going to break any laws, but they are not going to make a decision that puts their company in a worse position at a higher cost. While sovereignty gets [vendors] on the list, it doesn't assure that they get purchased," he told us. Earlier this month, Gartner predicted that by 2029, more than 90 percent of EU organizations will have a digital sovereignty strategy, but argued that a fully sovereign technology stack remains out of reach. "The global technology supply chain is too interconnected, and many critical dependencies cannot be replaced at a commercially viable scale," said Bettina Tratz-Ryan, VP analyst at Gartner. ®

item.title: The SE 3 is the Apple Watch most people should buy on Black Friday
item.description: The SE 3 adds an always-on display to Apple’s budget-friendly wearable. | Photo: Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge During Black Friday, the Apple Watch SE 3 is on sale in the 40mm / GPS configuration at Amazon , Walmart , and Target starting around $179 ($70 off), $20 less than its previous lowest price. The 44mm variant, meanwhile, is on sale at Amazon , Walmart , and Target starting at around $209 (also $70 off), also beating its previous low by $20. Apple Watch SE 3 Where to Buy: $249 $179 at Amazon (40mm, GPS) $249 $179 at Walmart (40mm, GPS) $279 $209 at Amazon (44mm, GPS) Despite having launched over a year ago, the Apple Watch SE 3 is still the Apple Watch model we recommend for most people. It includes many of the trademark features of higher-end Apple Watch models like the Series 12, including an always-on display, double-tap and wrist flick gestures, fast-charging, and on-device Siri. The compromise is that the SE 3 lacks some of the more advanced health features found on more expensive models, like blood oxygen and EKG sensing. item.title: UN warns of worsening hunger in northern Nigeria, 15 other areas
item.description: By Enitan Abdultawab The United Nations has warned of worsening hunger across 16 regions of the world over the next six months, identifying northern Nigeria, Sudan, South Sudan, Somalia and Yemen as areas facing the highest risk of acute food insecurity. The warning was contained in a joint report by the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) and the World Food Programme (WFP), which attributed the growing food crisis to armed conflicts, climate extremes, economic shocks and declining humanitarian assistance. The report, released on Friday, covers the period from December 2026 to May 2027 and cautioned that conditions could deteriorate further in several African countries as conflict and extreme weather events continue to disrupt livelihoods and food production. It identified Sudan and South Sudan as countries where famine remains a plausible risk, particularly in parts of North Darfur. The agencies also expressed concern over rising political violence, noting that incidents had increased by more than 15 per cent compared with the same period last year. The development, according to the report, has triggered significant displacement in recent months, particularly in South Sudan and Yemen, further worsening the humanitarian situation. It also highlighted a sharp decline in humanitarian funding to the five countries facing the highest levels of concern. According to the agencies, humanitarian assistance to the countries fell by nearly two-thirds between 2022 and 2025, dropping from $5.1bn to $2bn. “While conflict, economic shocks, climate extremes and access constraints have remained the primary drivers of these crises, declining humanitarian resources have reduced the capacity to sustain gains and mitigate worsening conditions,” the report stated. The agencies warned that previous humanitarian interventions had helped prevent famine in affected areas, but the improvements were often temporary, with severe food insecurity returning within a few years. Other areas classified as facing very high concern include Afghanistan, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Palestine and Haiti. The report noted that gang violence in Haiti had displaced about 1.5 million people and disrupted humanitarian access, while the Democratic Republic of Congo continues to grapple with an Ebola outbreak. Chad, Uganda, Southern Africa and the Central American Dry Corridor were also added to the list of hunger hotspots. The agencies warned that the impact of El Niño could worsen food production in several of these regions, particularly through irregular rainfall, drought and flooding. They estimated that about 49 million additional people could be pushed into acute food insecurity by the end of 2027 as a result of the particularly intense El Niño conditions expected to persist into next spring. “El Niño-related rainfall deficits and elevated temperatures have already contributed to crop losses in the Central American Dry Corridor and Eastern Africa, while also threatening the up

item.title: Israel Olaleye: How Can Young Nigerians Buy Land & Properties Legitimately Today?
item.description: Young man with a hard hat holding a red for sale sign outside a building by Pavel Danilyuk for Pexels . My parents’ generation mostly bought land the way their parents did. Someone in the family knew someone in the village. An uncle walked the boundaries. The community remembered who owned what, and if anything went wrong, you had a face to go back to. However, my generation buys land on Instagram. I do not say that to mock anyone. I sell land for a living. When I started in real estate sales in 2023, two years after finishing a Mathematics degree at the University of Ibadan, I assumed buyers would care most about price and location. They do care. But what I hear most often is fear, dressed up as questions. Can I trust you? Is this land real? What happens if I miss a payment? After I pay, will someone come and ask me for more money? A prospective buyer once asked me, before anything else, whether community or family payments would follow after she paid for her plot. She was not asking about the land. She was asking whether the price I quoted was the real price. She had good reason to ask. Lagos State’s Property Protection Law of 2016 made it an offence to demand levies for construction on someone else’s property. Yet the same law still allows a land-owning family, with the family head’s authority, to collect a customary fee for possession, the payment many people know as a “foundation levy”. So the honest answer to her question is not a simple yes or no. It depends on the land, the family, and what has been written down. Most first-time buyers have never been told any of this. That is the gap I keep coming back to. Nobody taught us how to buy land. We learned how to save. Some of us learned how to invest in stocks, crypto or a side business. But land, the asset our parents spoke about with the most respect, has no manual. The people who used to stand in for the manual–the uncle, the community, the family lawyer everyone trusted–are often not part of how we buy anymore. So we improvise. A prospect once told me she had gone through my Instagram page carefully before she agreed to speak with me. She was checking whether I was consistent, whether my posts matched what I said on the phone, whether I had been around long enough to be real. I was flattered. Then I was worried. Because if a social media page has become part of a buyer’s due diligence, then a polished page has also become one of the easiest ways to deceive her. Instagram cannot tell you who owns a piece of land. Only a search at the land registry, done by your own lawyer, can begin to tell you that. Instagram cannot tell you whether a plot sits under government acquisition or on a planned road. A surveyor who charts the coordinates and checks them against official maps can. No number of testimonials replaces a written contract that states what you are paying for, what you are not paying for, and what happens if a payment is missed. None of this is complicated. It is just not taught. The i

item.title: Astronomers watch a red giant star greedily devour a stellar 'Bao bun' before erupting: 'We couldn't quite believe our luck'
item.description: null Astronomers witnessed the spectacular cosmic indigestion that resulted from a red giant star that devoured a stellar Bao bun in the form of its smaller companion star. That isn't a random comparison. The cannibal star, which is 350 times bigger than the sun, is nicknamed "Big Bao," while its unfortunate companion had the nickname "Little Bao." The cute cosmic monikers come from the fact that this destructive merger event has been designated AT2025abao. A Bao bun might be a little snack for a human, but this red giant star made a real meal out of Little Bao. This cannibalistic event was tracked by a wide array of ground- and space-based telescopes, including NASA space missions NEOWISE, SPHEREx, and the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), as well as the W. M. Keck Observatory in Hawaii. The conclusion of the event AT2025abao was marked by a massive eruption witnessed in Oct. 2025 by two instruments at Caltech's Palomar Observatory: the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) and the Wide-field INfrared Transient ExploreR (WINTER). "The excitement was real," team member Viraj Karambelkar of Columbia University said in a statement sent to Space.com via email. "We couldn't quite believe our luck. With detailed observations for several years before the merger, for the first time, we now have an unprecedented glimpse of the conditions that lead to such cosmic events." Reconstructing a violent cosmic collision The story of AT2025abao began when astronomers detected a bright flash in the nearby Andromeda galaxy , a region where scientists hadn't expected to see a cosmic explosion. Responding to this unexpected flash, Karambelkar and colleagues set about investigating its cause with a plethora of telescopes. This led to them seeing a slow and continuous brightening over the course of two years, They determined the cause of the flash was a rare stellar merger, the luminous red nova now designated AT2025abao. They linked this to a star called WNTR23bzdiq / WTP19aalzlk that had been observed steadily brightening since 2019 after being stable for the preceding 30 years. Thus, the team determined that at the heart of the event is a red giant, a star that puffs out to hundreds of times its original size after it runs out of hydrogen in its core. The team theorizes that Big Bao, with a mass seven times greater than the sun, expanded so rapidly and violently that it swallowed its smaller companion star. The unfortunate star, Little Bao, then spiraled into Big Bao's core in fewer than 10 orbits. "A couple of years back, we discovered a star that was gradually brightening. We took a closer look to discover a red giant, or a star that has started to expand toward the end of its life, just like our sun will one day," Karambelkar said. "Steady brightening was unusual, but even if something was stirring, no one expected to see an explosion in their lifetime, as these stars remain relatively stable for thousands of years." item.title: AI boom leaves network operators waiting up to 18 months for kit
item.description: The AI building boom is driving up optical networking equipment prices and stretching delivery times to as much as 18 months, according to network operator RETN. RETN says that network operators and telcos are now directly competing with AI datacenters for chips and other components. As Reg readers will be aware, memory prices have soared by four or five times over the past year or so, but RETN says optical networking equipment prices have risen by around 50 percent since the start of 2026. Worse are the extended delivery times, with optical network kit that used to arrive within three months now taking 12 to 15, and some orders taking up to 18 months. This is as bad as, if not worse than, the shortages during the pandemic, when chip supply problems left network vendors unable to fulfill orders . The issue now is that because of the AI boom, demand is outpacing supplies. In its report, "AI, Connected," RETN says developers building outside established datacenter hubs may need to involve network carriers two to five years before opening. The sudden demand for network kit from hyperscalers and AI campuses is only one factor, RETN says. Raw material shortages, skilled labor shortages, energy constraints, geopolitical tensions, and logistical challenges are also compounding the issue. However, it concedes that many carriers didn't help themselves by previously postponing network upgrades to cut expenditure. That work has now become unavoidable at the worst possible time. Network diversity is now seen as a must-have, the report says. Where customers were once satisfied with two routes to long-haul destinations, they expect operators to provide four or more redundant routes now. The aim is to prevent a single failure from taking down critical services. Multiple connections are only useful protection if they avoid shared physical failure points, such as the same ducts or cable routes. A diverse circuit might cost €1,800 ($1,975) a month instead of €600 ($658), it claims, but an outage could prove far more costly. RETN also says AI datacenters are moving away from populated areas to remote locations, where access to suitable land, power and water may be easier to come by. Hyperscalers are building in the Nordics, where land is affordable, the climate is cooler, and plenty of renewable energy is available. Remote sites may lack the fiber infrastructure needed to connect them to other datacenters and customers. The Register reported on this issue earlier this year. For sites close to cities, developers often fund the fiber themselves, which adds just a few percent to the total project cost. But over longer distances, the case becomes harder to make, and carriers are understandably reluctant to build a long-haul route to serve a single remote site. item.title: British social security system techies yank services offline following 'cyber incident'
item.description: The UK's Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) has taken some services offline after detecting a "cyber incident," but says regular benefit and pension payments are unaffected. The department announced the precautionary shutdown on Friday morning. "We have taken some DWP online services offline as a precaution after we identified a cyber incident affecting our systems," it said. "We are working closely with the National Cyber Security Centre and Government Cyber Coordination Centre (GC3) to investigate and to bring services back online as quickly as possible and to minimize any disruption. "Regular benefit and pension payments are not affected and will be paid as normal. If an online service you need is unavailable, please try again later. As always, we will never message you to ask for bank details or ask you to click on links." The Register contacted both the DWP and NCSC for more information. The DWP declined to comment beyond the statement issued publicly. GC3 coordinates responses to incidents affecting government. The Government Cyber Unit leads the wider Government Cyber Action Plan, backed by more than £210 million. It is led by the government CISO, Bella Powell. Officials have not commented on any of the usual details one would expect from a cyber incident disclosure, including the specific services that were downed, when they are expected to return, or whether any data is thought to be compromised, even at this early stage. The UK government has also been criticized recently for investing heavily in AI cyber defenses, while the issue of legacy and aging IT continues to be neglected in the background. It announced at the end of October that it was throwing £130 million at AI cyber defense technology , as part of a wider £600 million cross-government AI spending spree announced by the Treasury. ExfilSquad recently claimed to have stolen around 607,000 records from the Department for Education and another 114,000 from the Police National Legal Database. ®

item.title: New Scientist Book Club: How urine changed the course of human history
item.description: A detail from Joseph Wright’s 1771 painting The Alchemist Discovering Phosphorus, showing Henning Brand in 1669 Science History Images/Alamy Imagine you could boil the development of science down to a single ingredient. A magical, mystical compound that transformed human history. Of course, science doesn’t work that way; even if breakthroughs shift the paradigm of our understanding, discovery doesn’t progress like a tech tree in a computer game, but as an interweaving tapestry of complementary and competing ideas and experimentation. Theories can bubble under the surface for centuries, overlooked because of politics or failure to realise their implications, while innovations can emerge from taking an idea in one industry and transplanting it to another. But, for a moment, try and picture what just one such ingredient could be. What would you pick? For centuries, in medieval Europe, alchemists quested for the “Philosopher’s Stone” that would finally help them achieve their dreams of transmutation. It was a search doomed to failure from the very beginning. And yet, a far better idea was under their noses – or, rather, their underpants – the entire time. My pick? Urine has a strong case for being the most transformative substance in human history. Free newsletter Sign up to Book Club Sign up to newsletter The development of civilisation was built on chemistry. It required the first chemical reaction we mastered – fire – to keep us warm, cook our food and smelt ores. But leatherwork played an equally key role. Urine is a source of urea, which bacteria can break down into ammonia, granting early humans easy access to a base that could soften organic matter and tan hides. Across the world, leatherwork became the cornerstone of survival for every civilisation, from the Americas to Europe, Africa and Asia: even cultures that didn’t develop a bronze age, such as the Aztec, or skipped it entirely, as seen in Sub-Saharan Africa, relied on leatherwork for clothes, structures, industry and commerce. Advertisement If the power of pee helped build civilisation, it would go on to be foundational in its upkeep. In ancient Rome, urine was so useful for laundries to keep togas whiter-than-white that Emperor Vespasian levied a tax on draining urinals. When his son complained, Vespasian’s response was blunt: pecunia non olet , money doesn’t stink. Part of the funds were used to build the Colosseum in Rome, today recognised as one of the wonders of the world. The magic of urine filtered into what would become chemical science, too. Cheimeia , the artisanal trade secrets and recipes found in Alexandria, Egypt, that would later give rise to alchemy, recognised the value of urine. In the Leiden Papyrus X , part of a cluster of the only original manuscripts on alchemy’s origins we still have, you can find a recipe for faking gold using polysulfides. item.title: Read an extract from The Age of Alchemy by Kit Chapman
item.description: The New Scientist Book Club is reading The Age of Alchemy in December “ A handful of lime and another of sulfur in fine powder. Place them in a vessel containing strong vinegar or the urine of a small child. Heat it from below, until the liquid appears like blood. Advertisement Decant this properly, and use. ” Unknown, Leiden Papyrus X , c. 300 CE In 1827, amid the dark, silent balm of an Egyptian night, a graverobber pulled a treasure from the sands. At first, the raider was frustrated; scavenging the tombs near Thebes, he had hoped to uncover a priceless heirloom, or a nugget of gold that would sparkle with lustre in the starlight. Instead, he had found only a clutch of rolled scrolls, made of papyrus and sealed against the elements. For a moment, he considered casting the documents aside and leaving them for the desert. Then greed got the better of him. Westerners loved all things Egyptian, he reasoned. Since the French had arrived with Napoleon, the new field of “Egyptology” had swept the continent, capturing the imagination of scholars and the wealthy. It was almost as popular as the new science of “chemistry”. Surely, if he took his find to the market, he’d find some gullible fool willing to buy it. The buyer’s name was Jean d’Anastasy, and he was anything but a fool. Born in Greece as the son of a Damascus merchant who had won and lost his fortune in the Napoleonic Wars, d’Anastasy had used his family’s connections to set himself up as a grain merchant in Alexandria, before scheming his way into being named the local Consul General for Sweden and Norway. Free newsletter Sign up to Book Club Sign up to newsletter When d’Anastasy wasn’t trading – or rescuing enslaved girls during the Greek War of Independence against the Ottoman Empire – he ran a side-hustle, “procuring” relics from Ancient Egypt and selling them to the salons of Europe: statues to the British Museum in London; rings and jewels to the Louvre in Paris; even a pair of sphinxes that still sit on the banks of the Neva River in St Petersburg. He quickly saw the value of the papers, paid for them, and shipped them back to Europe. Some went to Stockholm, and some to Leiden University in the Netherlands. Among the Leiden trove was one of the most remarkable finds in history: a papyrus scroll with a list of recipes, each with crystal-clear instructions written in Greek. While we have damaged cuneiform tablets and later copies of older works, the Leiden Papyrus X , written around 300 CE, is the oldest surviving alchemy book in history. It is a guide for Egyptian artisans to create wondrous riches, seemingly out of nothing. There are methods on how to polish silverware, cheap alternatives for making knock-off purple robes, and how to create gold lettering by mixing saffron and tortoise bile. item.title: Royal Navy orders £142M in minehunting drones from US supplier
item.description: Britain's Royal Navy is investing £142 million ($185 million) in underwater drones to tackle sea mines, but the contract has gone to an American defense supplier. The Ministry of Defence (MoD) says that the UK's ability to protect vital sea routes will be strengthened through the procurement of these Uncrewed Underwater Vehicles (UUVs). These will form part of the Royal Navy's move toward a " Hybrid Navy " comprising a mix of crewed, uncrewed, and autonomous platforms in order to meet future challenges. The UUV selected for the job is the REMUS 620 , built by Huntington Ingalls Industries (HII), the largest military shipbuilding company in the United States. HII has a facility at Portchester, on the south coast of England, but is still a US-owned company. We asked the MoD how the award fits its pledge to prioritize buying British wherever possible, and what share of the contract's value will support UK industry. The contract includes HII's Sea Launcher automated launch and recovery systems and will bring support services previously delivered overseas to the UK. HII says it will support 15 jobs, while the MoD identifies Portchester among the locations benefiting. HII says this is the largest international order in its 25-year history of supplying uncrewed systems. The MoD has previously acquired REMUS 100, REMUS 300, and REMUS 600 vehicles for mine countermeasure operations. The new vehicles will locate sea mines to support clearance operations and help keep shipping routes open. By using drones to comb a body of water for explosive devices, the Royal Navy's crews can be kept a safe distance from any potential immediate threat. Traditionally, this work has been conducted by specialist crewed ships such as the Hunt class or Sandown class , but these are being retired from service in favor of uncrewed systems. The Royal Navy also operates SWEEP , an uncrewed boat towing equipment that mimics a ship's magnetic, acoustic, and electric signatures to trigger mines from a safe distance. The new REMUS underwater vehicles can be sent ahead of other vessels to search beneath the surface, making minehunting operations safer, faster and more flexible, according to the MoD. "This investment strengthens our ability to protect freedom of navigation, which is critical to our security and our economy," said Defence Secretary Wes Streeting MP. Like others in the portfolio, REMUS 620 resembles a naval torpedo. It is capable of operating at depths of 600 meters and has an endurance of up to 110 hours on a single mission. The drones will be integrated with SeeTrack and Neptune software developed by SeeByte in the UK, which is already used by the Royal Navy. In trials announced in October 2025, a REMUS 620 demonstrated launch and recovery using a submerged test fixture replicating a Virginia-class submarine's torpedo tube. The work could enable submarines to deploy and retrieve underwater drones on future missions. ®

item.title: Volvo's big batteries: We drive its updated 2028 plug-in hybrids
item.description: Volvo provided flights from Washington, DC, to Copenhagen, Denmark, and accommodation so Ars could drive the XC60 and XC90 plug-in hybrids. Ars does not accept paid editorial content. COPENHAGEN, Denmark—If we lived in the world that Volvo’s product planners expected back when the current XC90 debuted in 2015 , both it and the smaller but related XC60 (which arrived in 2017) might have been the last of their kind as everything went electric . As we know, the future hasn’t turned out quite like that, especially in the critically important US market . At the same time, Europe and China are electrifying, which seems like an argument against spending resources on developing all-new replacements for models that might not have an eight-year lifespan in most markets. So instead, Volvo has given the XC60 and XC90 another lifecycle refresh. The exterior styling tweaks are minimal; the bigger three-row XC90 had already been given a new look last year, and the XC60 now gains a similar grille and the same matrix headlights, for instance. And that’s no bad thing—both were, and remain, handsome shapes that are popular with Volvo’s customer base. Instead, the Swedish automaker’s attention has been on bringing the technology up to date for model year 2028 standards. Which means a much bigger battery for the PHEVs, with sufficient capacity for a couple of days of daily driving for most of us before needing to be recharged. There’s also new, modern infotainment and interiors that are now even nicer to spend time in than before. Read full article Comments

item.title: Support team put in an emergency order for vodka – lots of vodka – to bring PCs back online
item.description: The end of the working week is often enough to drive tech support people to drink, which is why The Register likes to get the party started early. Friday mornings bring a new installment of On Call – the column in which we share your stories of doing whatever it takes to keep tech running. This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Bruce," who told us that in the mid-2000s he worked for a global radio station. "We used to have about 30 PCs, all running slightly different radio shows depending on the time zone where we broadcast," he explained. The PCs were old clunkers running Windows 95 long after Microsoft ended support for the OS. Management knew the machines needed replacing, but funding was probably another year away. "We had to coax them on till then," Bruce wrote. "And by coax, I mean we were buying RAM on eBay because nobody sold the 4MB sticks we needed anymore." Thanks to the tender ministrations of Bruce and his colleagues, the PCs kept humming and the radio stations stayed on the air. Until a lovely spring Tuesday, when Bruce and his crew enjoyed a bucolic cup of tea in the first real sunshine of the season and received a call informing them that one of the stations was down. One of Bruce's mates figured a cranky old PC probably just needed a reboot and headed off to fix it while the rest of the team enjoyed their tea. And then the phone rang again to report another outage, so Bruce and the entire crew went back to work, chatting about which switch or other shared device could have taken out two PCs. When they arrived in the office, the chap who had gone to reboot the first PC ran in and announced that the computer room had flooded. Bruce and his teammates ran into that room and found dirty brown water all over the floor, walls, ceiling, and the racks holding the ancient PCs. "Water was even spraying out of the front fans of the last two PCs that were still working," Bruce told The Register . "After a lot of shouting words unfit to print, we all got to work ripping them out, shutting down what we could that looked to be working, and started lining them up outside in the car park," Bruce wrote. "Some of us then got to work stripping them down into component parts, others washed them down with isopropanol." As the isopropanol supply dwindled, one of the team arranged an urgent delivery of vodka. "Luckily, it was a gloriously sunny day, so we quickly rinsed the PCs and left them to dry, strewn all over the car park," Bruce wrote. By this stage, he and the team were all filthy and exhausted. With the stations still offline, they had to rebuild the PCs and get them running again. "We only lost two sticks of RAM, one sound card, and a power supply," Bruce wrote. The culprit turned out to be a new hire on the facilities team who, while touring the building, had turned a random tap to see what would happen. "It released water from a stagnant iron tank that sat there rusting away for years," Bruce wrote. For reasons nobody understood, the tan

item.title: AWS adds virtual iPhones to its cloud
item.description: AWS now offers two new types of cloudy computers: emulated Androids and simulated iPhones. The cloudy colossus announced both virtual offerings on Wednesday. They’re part of its Device Farm service, which previously saw AWS offer developers the chance to test their software on actual iOS and Android devices that reside in the Amazonian cloud. AWS will now also host virtual devices running Android and iOS. AWS touts the virtual mobile devices as superior to physical devices. “With virtual devices, you can shift testing left to stages that need high speed and volume, such as pull requests, code merges, and smoke tests, and keep real devices for later stages that need high fidelity, such as regression and release testing,” the cloudy business unit argues in its launch announcement. AWS also says developers can get to work faster on a virtual iPhone or Pixel. “Virtual devices running the latest device and OS typically start in seconds, and others start in around a minute,” the outfit argues. That may sound appetizing, but Amazon’s menu of virtual devices is short and bland. When The Register logged on as an AWS user, the only emulated Android phone listed was a Google Pixel 10, running Android 15, 16, or 17. An emulated Pixel tablet running Android 17 is also on the menu. At the time of writing, we could find only a virtual iPhone 16, running iOS 18.6, 23.61, and 27.0. Analyst firm Counterpoint’s list of the world’s top 10 best-selling smartphones in Q2 of 2026 does not include a single Pixel device. The iPhone 16 occupies 10 th place. iPhone 17 models occupy the first, second, third, and seventh place on the list. AWS might excite more developers if it adds emulators for the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra, Galaxy A07 4G, A17 5G, A17 4G, and Galaxy S26, as they occupy the fourth, fifth, sixth, eighth and ninth places on Counterpoint’s list. Amazon’s choice of a Pixel tablet is also an oddity given analyst firm IDC doesn’t list Google among its top five tablet vendors . Amazon does offer physical Galaxy A17 devices and three versions of the iPhone 17. But Device Farm doesn’t offer any foldable devices, meaning developers struggling to wrap their heads around the iPhone Duo will need either ask Apple for a loaner or shell out $2,000 to acquire one. At least developers don’t have to change behavior to access the few virtual devices AWS offers, as existing Device Farm APIs and test frameworks will work on real or notional machines. ®

item.title: Shivelyuch Socked In
item.description: Earth Observatory Science Earth Observatory Shivelyuch Socked In Earth Earth Observatory Image of the Day EO Explorer Topics All Topics Atmosphere Land Heat & Radiation Life on Earth Human Dimensions Natural Events Oceans Remote Sensing Technology Snow & Ice Water More Content Collections Global Maps World of Change Articles Earth Matters Blog Blue Marble: Next Generation EO Kids Mission: Biomes About About Us Subscribe 🛜 RSS Contact Us Search In the same way that Shivelyuch (also called Shiveluch) frequently displays volcanic activity, it is also chronically obscured by clouds. When the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 captured this image on November 8, 2026, clouds encroached on the snowy mountain on Russia’s Kamchatka Peninsula . But they hovered beneath the volcano’s 3,283-meter (10,771-foot) peak, leaving a clear opening over its caldera and northern upper slopes. The upper reaches of Shivelyuch feature a caldera 9 kilometers (5.6 miles) wide that is open to the south. A lava dome , formed by vents extruding viscous magma, appears as a dark area within it. Lava domes on Shivelyuch go through cycles of growth and collapse, with collapses sometimes setting off fast-moving avalanches of hot ash and rock called pyroclastic flows . In November 2026, effusive eruptions of lava and explosive activity at Shivelyuch had been ongoing for months , according to reports from the Kamchatka Volcanic Eruption Response Team (KVERT). And despite frequent cloudiness, satellites regularly detect thermal anomalies from the volcano. On the day of this image, KVERT reported that a plume of resuspended ash drifted 120 kilometers (75 miles) to the east. That kind of activity is relatively tame for the mountain. Explosions from Shivelyuch periodically send ash several kilometers up into the atmosphere, where it can travel great distances and pose risks to aircraft . In July 2026, an ash plume rode the jet stream over the Bering Sea into Alaskan airspace, according to news reports , prompting the cancellation of multiple flights.
